newsitem.title: SPAIN: Basque group ETA admits it killed politician.
newsitem.headline: Basque group ETA admits it killed politician.

text.p: The Basque separatist group ETA claimed responsibility on Wednesday for the killing of a young Spanish politician which sparked national outrage.

"ETA assumes, through this communique, total responsibility for the arrest (July 10), and later execution after the 48-hour deadline passed (July 12), of the Popular Party member and Ermua town councillor Miguel Angel Blanco," it said in a statement published in the radical Basque newspaper Egin.
In the statement given to Egin, ETA's usual mouthpiece, the group said it "assumes...and will assume the consequences of the conflict...as crude and painful as they may be".

Two days after kidnapping the 29-year-old Blanco, the guerrillas shot him in the head after the government refused its demand to immediately move ETA prisoners scattered around the country to the Basque region.

The kidnap had been pinned on the rebel group from the day Blanco disappeared, when a caller contacted Radio Egin in the name of ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) and laid out the group's demands. However, until now, ETA had not officially admitted the killing.

ETA, which has killed around 800 people in a violent campaign for a Basque state over the past 29 years, reiterated on Wednesday that it was ready to lay down its arms if the government met its demands for independence.
Millions of Spaniards, incensed by the assassination of Blanco, an ordinary, low-ranking functionary, took to the streets last week in a display of anger.

Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, head of the Popular Party to which Blanco belonged, led marches in the Basque region and the capital Madrid. His party has planned a memorial service for Wednesday evening.
Three people suspected of belonging to a pro-ETA youth group were arrested on Wednesday after they attacked an employment office in the Basque regional capital Vitoria.
Faced with growing public opposition after Blanco's killing, ETA said in its statement on Wednesday that Spain had "created collective hysteria" aimed at criminalising the Basque separatist movement.
Egin said the statement differed from previous rebel communiques in that it was addressed to Spaniards and written in Spanish rather than in the Basque language Euskera.

Wednesday's statement followed two days of protests by ETA supporters angered by the death of one of their imprisoned militants, found hanged in his cell in an apparent suicide on Sunday. They blamed the government for his death.
On Wednesday, some 4,000 people paid silent tribute to the dead prisoner, Juan Carlos Hernando. They carried a banner saying: "Justice and freedom are the road to peace."

The Basque regional government has banned two demonstrations called by ETA's political wing, Herri Batasuna, in support of ETA. The party respected the order, calling off a march planned for last weekend, but has sought court permission to hold it this Sunday.
With anti-ETA sentiment still running high, authorities fear the demonstration could provoke street clashes.
